content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper, as the authors described, is working on zero-shot classification tasks. For the proposal, the authors propose to employ hyper-networks to generate a classifier using the category (textual) modality for the visual modality. The authors describe how they design the hyper-networks (if I understand this part correctly). In the experiments, the authors verify the effectiveness of the proposed method with a very uncommon experiment configuration.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

This paper is willing to challenge the zero-shot performance of the CLIP model, analytically and experimentally.

Weaknesses

To generate the classifier with a hyper-network is not a new idea, there are many studies using the hyper-network to achieve few-/zero- shot learning, for example, the following studies employ this idea, to name a few.

[1] Yin, Li, Juan M. Perez-Rua, and Kevin J. Liang. "Sylph: A Hypernetwork Framework for Incremental Few-shot Object Detection." 

[2] Zhao, Dominic, et al. "Meta-learning via hypernetworks." 

[3] Ponti, Edoardo Maria, et al. "Towards zero-shot language modeling." 

The paper is poorly organized, in Section 3 the authors spend a lot of pages to spend how the hyper-network is built, while providing no explanation of the terms such as ''symmetries'', ''equivariance'', ''invariance'', etc. However, I have totally no idea how these properties affect the outcomes, the authors should at least provide some insights or ablation experiments on the hyper-networks structure.

The weirdest thing in this paper to me, is the authors employ the domain-specified pre-train model to do ``zero-shot'' learning, and the number of unseen categories is fixed at 20% of the categories. How could a method call itself a zero-shot learning model when it has been pre-trained on the same domain dataset (or even the same ModelNet) of the categories to be recognized? How could we pre-define the number of unseen categories for a zero-shot model?

It is unclear what is the permutation $\mathcal{P}$? If it functions as changing the input descriptions of the textual modality, how could it permutate the output of $f$?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity, quality, and novelty are pretty low as mentioned in the weaknesses.

The reproducibility is also very low due to the authors providing no information on the detailed network structures.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper barely contributes anything to the zero-shot community, therefore it is a clear rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper tackles the problem of zero-shot classification, where it proposes to estimate the classifier weights for the unseen classes from their text descriptions. Specifically, the authors propose to use a hyper-network, which consists of several combinations of FC layers, to compute the classifier weights from text embeddings. The authors offers an equivariant-invariant 
design principle of the hyper-network, where requires the last layer of the classifier to be invariant to the permutation of inputs, and the earlier layers to be equivariant to the permutations. The authors validate their idea with multiple zero-shot datasets and different formats of textual descriptions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The motivation is clear and well defined. 
2. The equivariant-invariant principle is intuitive and well explained.
3. The experiments are well designed, and the results are convincing.
4. Good and interesting studies on different formats of textual descriptions of unseen class (single word, multiple words, sentence, sentence with negative descriptions).

Weakness:
1. Novelty and significance. The idea of “learning classifier weights from texts” is not new and has been studied before (e.g., in [1][2]), though prior works might use different text models/embeddings. It is not clear what’s the key difference from these works. And this type of works is not compared in the paper. The idea of equivariant-invariant design seems incremental, and it is only studied on FC-based architectures. I am wondering if this design principle is generally important in other type of architectures, for example, transformer-type layers.
2. Mixed-form textual descriptions. I am curious how the model could be affected given mixed-format of textual descriptions (e.g., some are single words, some are sentences, etc). 
3. Typos. Missing closing parenthesis in Eq. 3; additional \tao before [W^{last}, W^{pen}] in Theorem 3.1; result of “1-layer  w.o. EV” for ModelNet40 Unseen in Table 5.

[1] Lei Ba, Jimmy, Kevin Swersky, and Sanja Fidler. "Predicting deep zero-shot convolutional neural networks using textual descriptions." Proceedings of the IEEE international conference on computer vision. 2015.

[2] Wang, Xiaolong, Yufei Ye, and Abhinav Gupta. "Zero-shot recognition via semantic embeddings and knowledge graphs." Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2018.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written and organized. The tables and figures are clearly presented. Novelty is discussed in the previous section. The authors promise in the paper to release their code for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies an interesting problem of how to learn classifier weights from textual descriptions for zero-shot classification. The experiments are well designed and demonstrate interesting results. The main concern is about the novelty from previous similar works on classifier generation, and the significance of the proposed equivariant-invariant design principle.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for zero-shot learning from textual descriptions of classes that is based on a hypernetwork. The model takes text descriptions of classes and outputs weights for a zero-shot classification model. The authors show their model achieves higher accuracy than a number of other methods on AWA, ModelNet40, and SUN datasets, using either class name texts, short class descriptions, or descriptions generated by a GPT model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- (S1) The proposed method is conceptually simple and the authors use a small architecture for experiments.   
- (S2) Experimental results indicate consistent improvement over a few other models on selected datasets

Weaknesses:
- (W1) The choice of datasets/settings used for evaluation: one could generally expect the class names of SUN and AWA (used by the authors) to be generally more discriminative than e.g. commonly used for ZSL but not by the authors, CUB and NAB datasets which contain classes much more granular and similar to each other (bird species) where one could expect that relying only on class names would work worse. As the type of text used in experiments is limited only to short class names or single-sentence descriptions it is unclear how well the approach would generalize even to datasets like CUB, NAB.
- (W2) Experiments with using descriptions generated from the GPT model do not seem to bring much insight. Comparing Table 3 and Table 2, it seems that these descriptions work generally worse than just relying on class names (AWA)
- (W3) Experiments with negative descriptions (Table 3): the authors motivate using negative descriptions of classes by a potential feature of being able to e.g. classify animals that e.g. “do not fly”. Although it’s true that one could classify the lack of such properties using negative text descriptions it seems overly complicated compared to just using a positive description (so without negation, e.g. “does fly”) and checking how much the model agrees (that model like DeViSE and CLIP can easily do). Finally, DEM model seems to achieve higher accuracy on negative descriptions (Table 3) than on GPT descriptions (Table 2) - the authors don’t discuss or explain that
- (W4) It seems (although not 100% clear to me) that the authors create their own splits of classes into seen/unseen that are different than commonly used splits proposed by:  
    Xian, Yongqin, Christoph H. Lampert, Bernt Schiele, and Zeynep Akata. “Zero-Shot Learning - A Comprehensive Evaluation of the Good, the Bad and the Ugly.” *ArXiv:1707.00600 [Cs]*, July 3, 2017. [http://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00600](http://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00600).  
    That makes comparisons more difficult. Depending on what exact classes end up in the unseen set and how closely they are related to any of the seen classes the ZSL classification might get easier or more difficult. Especially important that the authors use a ResNet-18 pre-trained on ImageNet which could potentially have some overlap with “unseen” test classes.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is relatively clearly written. The proposed method is based on prior works (hypernetworks) but it’s a novel approach for ZSL.  
The code is not shared (yet?).
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes an interesting method for zero-shot learning. However, despite reporting positive results, due to the experimental setup and choice of datasets used potential limitations and weaknesses of the proposed model might not be well studied/visible. Additionally, not all experimental results presented show much insight.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper tackles the problem of zero-shot learning. The proposed high-level approach is: train a hyper-network to predict the parameters of a $k$-way classification network from the textual descriptions of $k$ visual classes.  The layers of the hyper-network are designed to be either equivariant or invariant to their inputs. These properties ensure the ordering of the text descriptions input to the hyper-network is preserved for the predicted final classification layer. The predicted $k$-way classifier is applied to a standard image representation extracted from a deep learning network such as a ResNet etc.

The empirical results presented mainly show the benefit of this approach to create binary classifiers mainly based on image classification tasks such as 

Contributions:
1) The paper shows that hyper-networks can be applied successfully to a varied set of binary classification problems with non-trivial visual inputs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

* The set of experiments explored show that for building binary classifiers the hyper-network approach proposed appears to make meaningful predictions.

* The paper explores multiple classification problems and shows how the hyper-networks within the scope of the experiments explored are doing something meaningful.


Weaknesses:

* The presentation of the technical and implementation details are somewhat poor and lacking in detail. For example

 - The details of the equivariant and invariant layers are only given via figure 2. It would be good to have these also mathematically described in the main paper.
 
 - The details of training the hyper-network are somewhat sparse. So for example how are the training sets $S^{k_j}$ sampled from the seen classes? Is cross-entropy loss used for training? What optimizer was used? How long did training take?

 - It takes some sleuthing within in the paper to get the details of the architecture used in the hyper-networks and also the architecture of the predicted networks. It would be better if these details were easier to find. 

* Missing comparison to other zero-shot learning based methods using standard ZSL and GZL evaluation metrics

 - It is not clear how the results in section 4.1 and reported in table 1 are obtained. Is $k$-way classification with $k >2$? Or are multiple binary classifiers aggregated to perform the $k$-way classification? Or is the average performance of the multiple binary classifiers reported? 

 - The hyper-network is mainly trained to predict binary classifiers and it appears most of the experimental results also report numbers on binary classification. However, most of the (generalized) zero-shot methods report results on $k$-way classification where $k$ is the number of labels associated with the dataset. Does the paper's approach with predicting binary classifiers scale up to $k$-way classification either through aggregating multiple (one-Vs-one or one-Vs-all) binary classifiers or estimating one $k$-way network? How does the method perform given the standard evaluation of ZSL and GZSL for the SUN and AwA2 datasets.



* Missing ablation experiments, analysis and details (reported in table 5):

- How does increasing $k$ the number of classes predicted by the hyper-network affect performance?

- For the results in table 5 it is not entirely clear what "1-layer w.o. EV" corresponds to. Is it a fully connected layer that outputs k*d numbers (where d is the dimension of the ResNet-18 image feature)?

- For table 5 there is very little analysis of the results.  For example why does the performance drop so little for the "1-layer w.o. EV" for the experiments on AWA? Is this not a little concerning. 

---------------------

Comments:

- Think there are typos in the performance numbers quoted in table 5 as there are some single digit numbers and these ae consistent with the other performance numbers. 

* The AWA has been suspended because of copyright issues. I think the authors should use AWA2 instead of AwA to ensure AwA continues to be phased out.

* There is the  SUN dataset (SUN Database: Large-scale Scene Recognition from Abbey to Zoo, by Jianxiong Xiao; James Hays; Krista A. Ehinger; Aude Oliva; Antonio Torralba, at CVPR 2010) and the SUN attribute dataset which is a subset of the SUN dataset. In the paper the numbers quoted are consistent with the SUN dataset, but the citation is to the SUN attribute dataset.  Which dataset is actually used in the SUN experiments?

* One of the standard datasets for GZSL is Cub. Why did the authors not perform experiments on this dataset?

* Training with negative descriptions is an interesting idea, but it does open up a whole can of worms of how to best use and exploit such anti-descriptions.  There are obviously  many more ways to describe how visual objects do not look or attributes they do not possess than by their "generative" descriptions. I do not think it is fair to compare with "generative" training approaches (GRaWD) as they implicitly assume the text descriptions are generative. But it is interesting to see that the hyper-network is relatively resistant to these labellings as is DEM. What happened to DeVise in table 3?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity and presentation of the work needs to be improved see above for comments.

Prior work does exist on tackling GZSL/ ZSL with meta-learning:
V. K. Verma, D. Brahma, and P. Rai, “Meta-learning for generalized zero-shot learning,” in Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artiﬁcial Intelligence, 2020
It would be interesting for the authors to comment on hyper-networks as a more attractive approach to meta-learning. 

Exact reproducibility might be a little hard due to the missing technical detail. The author though have committed their code and training/test splits after publication.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents an interesting idea to use hyper-networks with text inputs to predict classification layers for images after their image representations have extracted from a deep neural network. However, the experimental evidence is a somewhat lacking in demonstrating if this approach scales up to medium/large-sized classification problems. Also there are problems with the presentation of the technical material and experimental results as detailed above. These two reasons are the justification for my recommendation.

content.title: Text2Model: Model Induction for Zero-shot Generalization Using Task Descriptions
content.TL;DR: Produce a model for a classification task described in text at inference time without training; using equivariant hypernetworks
content.abstract:
We study the problem of generating a training-free task-dependent visual classifier from text descriptions without visual samples. This Text-to-Model (T2M) problem is closely related to zero-shot learning, but unlike previous work, a T2M model infers a model tailored to a task, taking into account all classes in the task. We analyze the symmetries of T2M, and characterize the equivariance and invariance properties of corresponding models. In light of these properties we design an architecture based on hypernetworks that given a set of new class descriptions predicts the weights for an object recognition model which classifies images from those zero-shot classes. 
We demonstrate the benefits of our approach compared to zero-shot learning from text descriptions in image and point-cloud classification using various types of text descriptions: From single words to rich text descriptions.
